newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-EU seeks agreement on cross-border payments.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-EU seeks agreement on cross-border payments.

text.p: The European Union will try in the coming weeks to bridge differences over draft legislation to make bank transfers within the 15-nation bloc safer, quicker and possibly cheaper.

At issue is what EU institutions see as the banking industry's inability to make voluntary improvements to the way small sums of money for such things as magazine subscriptions or foreign-holiday deposits are transferred.
The EU Council of Ministers and the European Parliament -- which decide together on legislation affecting the bloc's single market -- agree on the facts, but not the solution.
That is why representatives of the two institutions and the European Commission will meet on October 10 to hammer out their differences on proposed legislation covering credit transfers.
Under EU rules, a conciliation committee on the issue must reach a compromise within six weeks of starting its meeting.

In November 1994, following long-standing complaints from consumers organisations, the European Commission proposed that banks should execute cross-border payment orders within six working days, not charge both the sender and the receiver of money for the service and be made liable for lost transfers.

EU finance ministers agreed in December 1995 that the draft directive should cover payments below 25,000 European currency units ($31,250) to be increased to 30,000 Ecus after two years of implementation.
But the parliament -- the EU's only directly elected body -- wants the minimum coverage to be 50,000 Ecus arguing with the need to protect small businesses as well as individuals.
Ireland, which took over the six-month EU presidency in July, is aiming to get a deal at 35,000 Ecus from the date of entry into force of the directive, a diplomat said.
But just when this happens is another point of contention between EU ministers and the parliament.

EU sources said the most likely compromise was for the directive -- which must be transposed into national laws -- to come into force at the same time as the introduction of a single European currency in January, 1 1999.

The most difficult issue remains, however, the level of banks' liability for lost transfers. EU ministers agreed banks should be obliged to refund a minimum of 10,000 Ecus only, due to fears a higher amount would have a prejudicial effect on credit institution's solvency requirements.
But the parliament wants to double this.
An attempt by the Irish presidency to find a compromise at 15,000 Ecus met with the stiff opposition of France, Germany, Belgium, Austria and the Netherlands, a Commission source said.
European banks have criticised the plan saying small value cross-border transfers cost them a lot of money because they usually involve several banks and a lot of paper work.

But Mario Monti, the European commissioner in charge of the EU's single market, argued that European citizens and small businesses, not only banks which can operate freely in the bloc, must also see the benefits of a borderless Union. $1 = 0.79 Ecus
